issue:
# Backup file_logger should store relative paths

h2. Summary

Backup {{file_logger}} should serialize a relative path (just the filename) rather than the absolute {{$CFG->backuptempdir/$backupid.log}}. 

The absolute path is host specific and ends up baked into the backup controller record and into the {{.mbz}} artefact, which makes backups non portable and causes restore code to blindly open whatever path was deserialized. Storing a relative path and rebuilding the full path on the fly using the current {{$CFG->backuptempdir}} fixes both.

h2. Background

This came out of [https://moodle.atlassian.net/browse/MDL-76288|https://moodle.atlassian.net/browse/MDL-76288|smart-link], which fixed {{backup_cleanup_task}} crashing when {{$CFG->backuptempdir}} had changed since the controller was serialised. {{file_logger::__wakeup}} now needs to also handle relative paths, this ticket adds that read-side support alongside switching the writer to produce relative paths.

issue:
# Event user_loggedout does not contain correct realuserid

It has taken some time to understand this issue, however, I think we've got it now.

If you are imitating an account, there is an issue with the fact the buffered writer (tool\log\classes\helper\buffered_writer) tries to retrieve the realuser just after it was destroyed.

Meaning the wrong information is written to the log in the end.

The issue is caused by the fact the $event->trigger() for the require_logout() takes place just after the session manager terminates the current session, meaning it has destroyed the data the buffered_writer wants to write, causing it to revert to null.

Aka, the wrong details eventually end up in the logs.

 

The fix is pretty simple, as it would be enough to just trigger the event before the session is terminated, which should make sure the realuserid is stored correctly while maintaining the rest of the flow.

# Forgot password tokens should be invalidated when account email address changes or a new token is requested

We should only be accepting tokens sent to an account's current email address, so when a user's email account is updated, we should invalidate tokens used in password reset (forgotten password) links sent to the old address. (It would be worth also having a look for  any other similar tokens that may need similar treatment.)

We should also be removing existing tokens if a new one is generated (ie another forgot password request for the account is received).

Given the (default) short life of such tokens and the fact that they are single use, these are fairly edge case, but is a valid fix to comply with security best practice. Taking that into account along with the low risk of being an exploitable issue, I've marked this as a security benefit, and not assigned a security level.

For consistency, we should also invalidate forgot password tokens if the password is changed, regardless of method..

# Navigation footer: Implement linear navigation exceptions for Previous/Next

Following the implementation of the core 'Previous' and 'Next' navigation buttons, we need to refine the logic to handle boundary cases within the course structure. This improvement ensures that the navigation remains logical and does not lead users into "dead ends" or redundant loops.

Specifically, we need to handle the start of course sections and the end of the course. At the first activity of a course, the “Previous” link should be suppressed to encourage a forward-moving flow within that module. At the final activity of the entire course, the “Next” link should be replaced with a clear "Back to course" link to return the user to the main course page for closure:

!image-20260430-132814.png|width=600,alt="image-20260430-132814.png"!

h3. 🎯 Required actions

* Update the navigation renderer to detect if the current activity is the first item in the course. If so, the “Previous” button should be hidden.
* Update the footer logic to identify the final activity in the entire course sequence. For the last activity, replace the standard “Next” link with a "Go to course" link as per the design prototype.
* Ensure the "Go to course" link correctly resolves to the course main page (course/view.php?id=x).
* Ensure that when the “Previous” button is hidden (at the first activity of a course), the remaining navigation elements (the “Next” button or "Go to course" link) maintain their correct alignment according to the prototype.

h3. (/) Acceptance criteria

* The “Previous” button is not displayed for the first activity of a course.
* The “Next” button is replaced by a "Go to course" link for the last activity of the course.
* Clicking "Go to course" successfully redirects the user to the main course page.
* The transition between these states is seamless and does not cause layout shifts in the sticky footer.
* Navigation logic respects hidden activities and access restrictions (e.g., if the "next" activity is hidden, the "Go to course" link should appear earlier if that activity is effectively the last one accessible to the student).

issue:
# Dashboard-class React/ESM pages load many small unbundled JS module files (investigate bundling/HTTP2)

h2. Problem statement

Dashboard-class pages built on Moodle's React/ESM pipeline (first found on /my/index.php during MDL-89636) load roughly 100 separate small ES module files as individual, unbundled HTTP requests. This is a platform-level characteristic of the ESM/design-system build output, not something specific to the dashboard: @moodlehq/design-system alone contributes about 31 of the files and is used site-wide wherever the design system appears, not just on this page.

Also, on HTTP/1.1, browsers cap concurrent per-host connections at roughly 6, so the ~100 files load in slow serial waves instead of in parallel, adding real, measurable time to any page built on this pipeline.

h2. Current behaviour

A single dashboard page load fetches close to 100 small ES module files (each roughly 1-3KB), none bundled. Breakdown from one real measurement: @moodlehq/design-system about 31 files (site-wide impact, biggest single contributor); @moodle/lms about 42 files (covers core_my's own dashboard components and pre-existing block_timeline view files); Bootstrap internals (util/dom submodules) about 14 files; floating-ui/popperjs/tabbable dependency chain about 9 files.

Some webservers are configured to serve HTTP/1.1 only.

ESM files are already served through a revisioned path ({{/esm/{revision}/{scriptpath}}}, see {{esm_controller.php}}), using the same revision-validity check as core's existing jsrev-based JS caching. When the revision is valid, the response gets a 1-year immutable {{Cache-Control}} header plus an ETag with 304 support; when invalid (or in dev mode), it falls back to a 2-second-expiry path instead. *Confirmed by this investigation: this caching is active and working correctly on a standard install* (see Findings below).

h2. Expected behaviour

This investigation should proceed in the following order, since the candidate mitigations interact and some may make others unnecessary:

# HTTP/2 (or HTTP/3) first: determine whether enabling it on a production-representative server config dramatically reduces or resolves the waterfall, and what server-side changes are actually required to get h2 negotiating correctly.
# Caching correctness second: confirm whether ESM files are being served with correct revision-based, long-term immutable caching (as already implemented in {{esm_controller.php}}) in the environment under test, and how much that changes the measured cost on a warm/repeat-visit basis versus the cold-cache baseline. Fix this if it is not behaving as designed, before evaluating bundling.
# Bundling last, and only if still needed after 1 and 2: re-assess whether bundling the ESM build output is still worth pursuing. HTTP/2 is explicitly designed to make many small parallel downloads competitive with (or better than) one large serial download, and bundling would work against the swizzle/theme-override mechanism, which deliberately keeps components as separate modules today. Any bundling recommendation should explicitly weigh that trade-off rather than defaulting to bundling as the fix.

Whichever mitigation(s) from steps 1-3 prove safe and quick to apply should be implemented as part of this issue. Anything that is a bigger undertaking (for example a full production HTTP/2 rollout) should be documented with the investigation's findings and filed as a linked follow-up ticket rather than blocking this one.

h2. Findings and resolution

*1. HTTP/2* -  A genuine PHP-FPM + mpm_event + mod_http2 build was measured: real HTTP/2 confirmed end-to-end ({{curl --http2}}, and the browser's Resource Timing {{nextHopProtocol}} reporting {{h2}} for every request). This is the single largest lever measured in this investigation. It is an infrastructure/webserver-layer change outside Moodle's own codebase (either a PHP-FPM + mpm_event backend migration, or - the standard, lower-risk production pattern - a fronting reverse-proxy/CDN edge that terminates HTTP/2 with the browser and speaks HTTP/1.1 to an unchanged backend); full guidance filed as MDL-89729.

*2. ESM caching* - confirmed already working correctly as designed, no code change needed. Cold-cache (first visit): 89 ESM requests, median last-ESM-response ~18.7s. Warm/repeat visit (normal reload): 0 of 89 ESM files re-transferred over the network (served from disk cache via the existing immutable {{Cache-Control}} + ETag), load event ~900ms.

*3. Bundling* - not pursued; confirmed an antipattern for the current architecture, not merely lower priority. The swizzle/theme-override mechanism works because each component resolves through its own bare specifier in the import map, so a theme can override one component by pointing that one specifier at a different file. Bundling multiple modules together removes that per-specifier override granularity. With caching already effective for repeat visits and HTTP/2 (or a shared cache, see MDL-89729) already addressing cold visits with no architectural cost, bundling's narrow remaining benefit does not justify breaking the override mechanism.

*4. Implemented (this issue)* - {{page_requirements_manager::get_import_map()}} now emits a {{modulepreload}} link for each concrete, active-theme import map entry - {{react}}, {{react-dom}}, {{tabbable}}, {{bootstrap/bootstrap.js}}, and the active theme's design-system bundle - so the browser can start fetching those foundational dependencies in parallel with page parsing instead of only discovering them one import-graph level at a time. The {{modulepreload}} links must be emitted _after_ the {{importmap}} script tag: browsers only honour an import map for bare-specifier resolution if it is registered before the first module-related resource is processed. Final, verified measurement (fresh isolated browser contexts, cold cache, Xdebug off, median of 3 runs, clean console, 89/89 ESM files on every run):
|| Configuration || Median cold-cache last-ESM-response ||
| HTTP/1.1, no modulepreload (original baseline) | 18,667 ms |
| HTTP/1.1, with the modulepreload fix | 17,856 ms (~4.3% faster) |
| HTTP/2 (PHP-FPM + mpm_event + mod_http2), with the modulepreload fix | 15,882 ms (~11% further, ~15% combined) |

No regression to swizzle/theme-override resolution ({{get_path_for_script()}} untouched) or existing {{import_map}}/{{esm_controller}} PHPUnit coverage. The PHP-FPM + mpm_event + mod_http2 stack itself was also validated against the existing PHPUnit external-services suites (redis, ldap) and Behat (non-JS and JS/Selenium), all passing except two failures independently reproduced as pre-existing under a plain mod_php control build (a solr status-check test blocked by this dev site's default curl-security host/port allowlist, and one AI-provider admin-modal Behat scenario) - neither caused by this issue's changes.

*5. Follow-up filed*: MDL-89729 (linked, Relates) documents the HTTP/2 production rollout (reverse-proxy/CDN termination recommended first, no backend change; PHP-FPM + mpm_event migration as the alternative for self-managed Apache, with the real numbers above), HTTP/3 (guidance only - automatic h2/HTTP-1.1 fallback via {{Alt-Svc}}, no separate Moodle-side work needed), and Varnish/CDN shared-cache guidance (a cookie-stripping fix for the {{/core/esm/}} path, since a shared cache's default cache-key hashing on the session cookie would otherwise fragment the cache per logged-in user, with a reference VCL snippet).

h2. Value

Faster page loads across every ESM/design-system-based page (not only the dashboard) by removing an HTTP/1.1 request-waterfall bottleneck that is currently platform-wide. The improvement should be concretely quantified before and after using real browser Navigation/Resource Timing metrics, not assumed.

h2. Scope

h3. In scope:

* determining whether HTTP/2 (or HTTP/3) materially closes the gap on a production-representative stack and what server config that requires (investigated first);
* confirming whether ESM files are served with correct revision-based, long-term caching in the environment under test, and fixing that if it is not behaving as designed (investigated second);
* measuring and documenting the ESM/module request waterfall using the methodology in the Testing Instructions field, across the above phases;
* only after the above, re-assessing whether bundling ESM build output is still needed, and whether it can be done without breaking swizzle/theme overrides;
* evaluating lower-cost request-level wins (keep-alive tuning, Early Hints/modulepreload) alongside the above;
* implementing whichever of the above mitigations is safely achievable within this issue based on the findings.

h3. Out of scope:

The narrow dashboard-only file consolidation already done under MDL-89636 (that was a local tweak, not a fix for this platform-wide issue); a full production HTTP/2 rollout or other infra-level server changes, if the investigation shows that is a bigger undertaking than fits this issue (file as a follow-up instead); redesigning the swizzle/theme-override system itself.

h2. Acceptance criteria

# HTTP/2 (or HTTP/3) is investigated first and measured following the methodology in the Testing Instructions field (XHProf-based profiling ruled unreliable and not used; browser Navigation/Resource Timing APIs used instead; Xdebug off during measurement; at least 3-5 repeated runs with the median reported); a documented recommendation is reached on how much it closes the gap. *Met* - see Findings above.
# ESM file caching behaviour is checked second: confirmed correct (valid revision, immutable long-term Cache-Control, ETag) or fixed if not, with cold-cache versus warm-cache measurements documented. *Met* - confirmed correct, no fix needed.
# Bundling feasibility is only assessed after 1 and 2, and the recommendation explicitly weighs HTTP/2's parallel-download model and the swizzle/theme-override constraint rather than defaulting to bundling. *Met* - not pursued, confirmed an antipattern.
# Findings are documented for each phase: per-run counts of ESM requests, nav.responseEnd, the dashboard AJAX call's start/end time, and the last ESM resource's responseEnd. *Met* - see comments for full per-run figures.
# Whichever mitigation(s) are determined to be low-risk and implementable within this issue are implemented, and the same measurement methodology shows a measurable reduction in load time and/or request count, with no regression to swizzle/theme-override behaviour. *Met* - modulepreload fix implemented and measured.
# Any larger-scope mitigation not implemented here (for example a full HTTP/2 rollout) is filed as a linked follow-up ticket with the investigation's findings attached. *Met* - MDL-89729.
# No regression in existing dashboard/ESM page functionality: existing Behat, PHPUnit, and Jest coverage for touched areas still passes. *Met* - see Findings above.

h2. Notes

Related background (context only, not separately re-investigated or modified by this issue): MDL-87830 (secondary navigation migrated to the design-system nav pill component), MDL-89294 (top navigation migrated to the design-system nav pill component), and MDL-88287 (Timeline block migrated to ESM + React) are prior work that moved components onto the ESM/design-system pipeline and are part of why the file count is now this high.

MDL-89636 already made one narrow, in-scope mitigation of its own (consolidating a couple of its own non-swizzled dashboard component files) - that is a local tweak, not a fix for this platform-wide issue.

# KDF() silently reduces large PBKDF2 iteration counts to weak 32-bit aliases

The SQL `KDF()` function reads its PBKDF2 iteration argument as a signed
64-bit integer and checks only that it is positive. It then narrows the value
to the 32-bit `int` expected by OpenSSL. As a result, iteration counts that
differ by 2^32 can derive exactly the same key.

In the reproduced release, requesting 4,294,968,296 iterations silently did
the work of 1,000 iterations; 4,294,968,297 similarly aliased to 1,001. An
application can therefore request a very large work factor but receive a key
derived with a much smaller one without any SQL error or warning.

h3. Steps to reproduce

Run this only against the pinned disposable container. Each high-value query
has a hard client timeout. Do not replace the values with `INT_MAX`, because
that would request prohibitive PBKDF2 work on an implementation that accepts it.

OWNER="edbf-report-$C-$$"
cleanup() {
  if docker inspect --format '{{ index .Config.Labels "io.encryptiondbfuzz.owner" }}' \
       "$C" 2>/dev/null | grep -Fqx "$OWNER"; then
    docker rm -f "$C" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
  fi
}
trap cleanup EXIT

docker run --detach --name "$C" \
  --label "io.encryptiondbfuzz.owner=$OWNER" \
  --env MARIADB_ALLOW_EMPTY_ROOT_PASSWORD=1 "$IMAGE"

READY=0
for i in $(seq 1 90); do
  if docker exec "$C" mariadb --protocol=socket -uroot -NBe \
       "SELECT @@port" 2>/dev/null | grep -qx 3306; then

done
test "$READY" -eq 1

# Performance regression after implementing MDL-60912

MDL-60912 (integrated in 5.0.7 / 5.1.4 / main) changed \core_completion\progress::get_course_progress_percentage() to call the new completion_info::get_user_activities_with_completion() instead of the lightweight get_activities().


For every course module with completion enabled, get_user_activities_with_completion() now constructs a \core_availability\info_module and calls filter_user_list(), which in turn calls capability_checker::get_users_by_capability('moodle/course:ignoreavailabilityrestrictions') on the module context.


This availability + capability resolution runs per module, per course, per request. On pages that summarise many courses via course_summary_exporter — Dashboard, Calendar block, Timeline block, Starred courses, My overview — the cost multiplies (courses × completion-enabled modules × capability resolution) and produces a noticeable performance regression compared with 5.0.6. The expensive work is also repeated because get_course_progress_percentage() is called multiple times per request for the same (course, user) pair (e.g. calendar/classes/external/event_exporter_base.php instantiates a new course_summary_exporter per event).


+*_This was anticipated during the MDL-60912 review (performance concern was raised in the comments) but no follow-up optimisation was integrated._*+



*Steps to reproduce*

# Site with completion tracking enabled.
# A user enrolled in many courses, each with several completion-tracked activities (with few or no availability/group restrictions — the common case).
# Load the Dashboard (or a page with the Calendar / Timeline / Starred courses blocks).
# Profile the request (e.g. $CFG->perfdebug = 15, or an APM/DB-query profiler).

Expected result
Course progress percentages are calculated with overhead comparable to 5.0.6; unrestricted activities do not incur per-module availability/capability resolution.


*Actual result*
Each completion-tracked module triggers an info_module + get_users_by_capability() resolution, repeated across courses and repeated per call within the same request, measurably increasing DB load and page render time.


*Affected code*

* completion/classes/progress.php — get_course_progress_percentage()
* lib/completionlib.php — get_user_activities_with_completion() (introduced by MDL-51447, used by MDL-60912)
* Callers via core_course\external\course_summary_exporter (Dashboard, block_calendar_*, block_timeline, block_starredcourses, block_myoverview, enrol/externallib.php, report builder completion formatter)



*Proposed solution*
Two complementary, behaviour-preserving optimisations (correctness of MDL-60912 fully retained):

# Fast path in get_user_activities_with_completion() — when a module has no availability rule (empty($cm->availability)), is not in separate-groups mode ($cm->groupmode !== SEPARATEGROUPS), and has no grouping restriction (empty($cm->groupingid)), the module is accessible to every enrolled user. Skip the info_module + capability_checker work and count it directly. This is mathematically equivalent to the existing slow path for unrestricted modules (the overwhelming majority). Modules that actually carry a restriction still take the full slow path, so hidden/unavailable/group-restricted activities continue to be excluded correctly.
# Per-request memoisation in get_course_progress_percentage() — cache the computed percentage per (course, user) in a MODE_REQUEST cache so repeated calls within one request (multiple exporters) reuse the result. Cheap pre-checks (is_enabled(), is_tracked_user()) stay outside the cache so capability/setting changes are always honoured. The cache key embeds $course->cacherev (so structural / visibility / availability / grouping changes invalidate it automatically), and the cache is purged in completion_info::internal_set_data() so completion-state changes within the same request are reflected.
No DB schema change, no version.php bump, no new cache definition, no new events/observers required.

Steps to reproduce

# Site with completion tracking enabled.
# A user enrolled in many courses, each with several completion-tracked activities (with few or no availability/group restrictions — the common case).
# Load the Dashboard (or a page with the Calendar / Timeline / Starred courses blocks).
# Profile the request (e.g. $CFG->perfdebug = 15, or an APM/DB-query profiler).



*At Moxis, we have already implemented a fix and it works. It keeps the fix from MDL-60912 but skips unnecessary steps and caches where relevant. I have added the patch for this issue as an attachment.*

issue:
# Implement OAuth 2 Server client manager class

To support an internal OAuth2 authorisation server within Moodle, we need a centralised management class to handle CRUD operations for OAuth2 clients, their associated secrets, and redirect URIs.

Scope:

* The class should implement methods that allow
** Fetching clients
*** by ID
*** by client identifier
** Updating a client (restricted to modifying administrative metadata: name, description)
** Revoking a client
** Reactivating a revoked client
** Permanent deletion of a client
** Generation of client secrets (including a logic to enforce a maximum active secret limit per user to 2)
** Fetching client secrets
** Revoking client secrets
** Fetching redirect URIs
** Creation of redirect URIs
** Removal of redirect URIs
** Validation of redirect URIs
* Unit test coverage

h2. Clarifications

* *Secret limit scope*: the maximum of 2 active secrets is enforced *per client*, not per user (a user may own multiple clients, each with its own limit of 2 active secrets).
* *Client revocation cascade*: revoking a client immediately revokes all of that client's active tokens and secrets (integrates with the revocation logic in MDL-88473), fully cutting off access rather than just blocking new token issuance.
* *Reactivation semantics*: reactivating a revoked client only restores the client record itself. Previously-revoked secrets and tokens remain revoked; the client must generate new secrets and go through authorization again to obtain new tokens.
* *Deletion precondition*: permanent deletion is only allowed once a client is already in a revoked state. This acts as a safety guard against accidentally destroying a live integration.
* *Redirect URI validation*: URIs must match exactly (no prefix/wildcard matching) and must use HTTPS, except for {{localhost}}/loopback addresses (to support native app development). No cap on the number of redirect URIs per client.
* *Class design*: all methods must be instance methods (not static), and the class is expected to be loaded via dependency injection (Moodle's {{\core\di}} container), not instantiated directly or accessed via static/singleton patterns.

h2. Acceptance criteria

# All CRUD/lifecycle methods listed above are implemented with the rules described in Clarifications.
# Secret generation enforces the per-client limit of 2 active secrets.
# Revoking a client cascades to revoke its active tokens and secrets.
# Reactivating a client does not restore previously-revoked secrets/tokens.
# Permanent deletion is rejected unless the client is already revoked.
# Redirect URI validation rejects non-exact matches and non-HTTPS URIs (except localhost/loopback).
# The class exposes only instance methods and is resolvable via dependency injection.
# PHPUnit test coverage for all of the above, including edge cases (secret limit exceeded, delete-before-revoke rejection, invalid redirect URI schemes, reactivation not restoring secrets).
